extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and critical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of reasoning: the relation between particular observations, general propositions (induction), and the syllogistic form for testing and applying generalizations. Focuses on when to reason from particulars directly and when to construct or interpret general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: All inference is from particulars to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions are merely registers of inferences already made; the real logical antecedent is the particular facts from which the general proposition was collected by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat general statements as summaries/short-hands of underlying observed instances. Recognize that when we conclude about an individual case (e.g., 'The Duke of Wellington is mortal'), the epistemic ground ultimately lies in remembered or recorded particulars, not in the abstract generality itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish inferring from registering
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the act of drawing an inference with the later act of recording or recollecting it; referring to a memorandum is not the origin of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an argument, ask whether the record (general statement) is being misread as the source of the inference. Use the notes/record only as a reminder of prior observations and warranted inferences, not as the primary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizations compress observations and inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition is an aggregate of particular truths — 'a comprehensive expression, by which an indefinite number of individual facts are affirmed or denied at once' — and is both a naming device and a vehicle for inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assessing general claims, ensure they reflect both observed instances and the inferences legitimately drawn from them; remember generalization is not mere naming but an inductive act that extends observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism as interpretation and consistency-check
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of the syllogism is to ascertain the meaning (testimony or will) of a witness or legislator, or to interpret our own memorandum of prior inductions; its rules help maintain consistency between specific conclusions and prior general directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syllogistic analysis to check whether an application of a general rule to a particular case conforms to the scope intended by the originator (observer, author, or legislator). Treat syllogisms as tools for interpretation rather than as the primary source of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use syllogistic form to reveal inconclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting an argument into an induction-to-generalization followed by syllogistic application often reveals cases where premises are insufficient, because the general form brings all potential parallel cases into view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt about an argument's validity, restate it as: (1) induction from particulars to a general principle, then (2) application of that principle to the case. Look for counterexamples within the general class to detect insufficiency (a reductio ad impossibile).

rubrics_metrics.name: State general principles in their broadest warranted form
rubrics_metrics.description: It is extremely important to ascertain and declare the general theorem in its broadest form of generality, to place before the mind the whole extent of what the evidence must prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming or reviewing a generalization, articulate its full scope so that evidence requirements are explicit. A broader statement helps uncover hidden counterinstances and avoids overstating what the evidence supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose direct particular-to-particular inference when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: In simple, familiar, or strongly experienced cases, we may legitimately reason at once from observed particulars to other particulars without passing through an explicit general proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow direct analogy-based or exemplar-based inferences in routine or well-understood contexts, but be cautious to limit claims to the similarity actually warranted by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer generalization when experience is limited or bias likely
rubrics_metrics.description: When the case is complex or our experience is limited (or when bias/wishful thinking may affect judgment), it's advantageous to form an induction to a general proposition and then apply it, because the general form makes defects in evidence more likely to be detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In uncertain or contentious inferences, demand a stated general principle and test it against known countercases before applying it to the target case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and definitions function as shorthand assumptions in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms and definitions are abridged statements or notices of particular assumptions we intend to make; demonstrations often actually assume the property in a particular instance rather than deriving it from an abstract axiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing demonstrations, check the particular assumptions instantiated in diagrams or examples; do not treat axioms/definitions as magical sources of evidence — they signal permitted assumptions for particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of syllogism are precautions for correct interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules for the syllogism are a set of precautions to ensure we read our records (general propositions) correctly and apply them consistently to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syllogistic rules as procedural checks: verify that categorical inclusion/exclusion and scope are read properly, and ensure the application matches the originally intended class markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware entrenchment of inadequately evidenced maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: A countervailing inconvenience of committing inductions to general maxims is that inferences made on insufficient evidence may become 'consecrated' and the mind cleaves to them by habit after particulars are forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly revisit and test general maxims against fresh or remembered particulars; encourage skepticism of long-held rules when their evidentiary basis cannot be recalled or defended.

rubrics_metrics.name: When premises are authoritative, resolve by hermeneutics
rubrics_metrics.description: If the general premises come from testimony or law (authority or legislator), the task is interpretive: determine whether the authority intended to include the present case by examining the marks by which intended cases are indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In legal, doctrinal, or testimonial reasoning, focus on exegetical questions: what did the source mean to cover? Apply hermeneutic criteria (language, context, indicia) rather than treating the syllogism as purely evidential.
